title: Howard Lutnick is one big problem for the Trump administration | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump stood by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday, but others in the administration must be wondering what will come next.

The last few days show how Lutnick could be a particular liability come January, when Democrats have subpoena power to scrutinize the administration’s many controversies.

And there has been no shortage of Lutnick-involved controversies, dating back to early last year, with the internal scrutiny of him reaching a potential inflection point amid the Nvidia scandal of the past week.

On Friday, for example, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unmistakably tossed Lutnickunder the busin a cable news interview — an extraordinary display of internal discord even by this administration’s own chaotic standards.

Bessent blamed Lutnick’s department for failing to block China from obtaining coveted Nvidia AI chips, by not putting a company at the center of the Nvidia scandal on an export blacklist.

“Commerce … has the pen,” Bessent said. “You would have to ask them about their internal processes.”

While some of Trump’s advisers havebegun discussingwhether Lutnick should be dismissed, the president told reporters on Monday while on his way to Asia — with Lutnick in tow — that he’s not considering replacing his Commerce secretary.

But theNvidia episodeis far from the first time Lutnick has caused the administration problems.

At the beginning of the second Trump administration, Lutnick — a billionaire — downplayed seniors missing their Social Security checks by suggesting only “fraudsters” would complain about that.

“My mother-in-law who’s 94 – she wouldn’t call and complain,” Lutnick said.

It was among the first weird and remarkably out-of-touch comments from an administrationstocked with billionairesthat has failed to feel Americans’ economic pain.

Earlier in March 2025, Lutnick also declared that Trump’s policies would be“worth it” even if they were to lead to an economic recession.

And also that month, Lutnick went on Fox News and encouraged people tobuy the stock of Tesla— even as Tesla CEO Elon Musk was serving in the administration running the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE. This appeared to violate government conflict of interest rules.

Another mainstay of Lutnick’s 2025 comments were his regular predictions that the economy wouldbe in fantastic shape in a matter of months— often around the end of that year or the start of 2026. Those conditions have yet to materialize. And the happy talk epitomized the failed economic promises that wound up haunting Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

Lutnick’s mouth was also a major liability once the administration’s Epstein problems began in mid-2025.

The biggest example is his false denials of his own ties to the late convicted sex offender.

In an October interview with a New York Post podcast, Lutnick said he vowed after a disconcerting 2005 encounter in Epstein’s home to “never be in the room with that disgusting person ever again.” Lutnick said that after that, he was “never in the room with him socially for business or even philanthropy.”

Except it turned out that he was. The Epstein files showed Lutnicksetting up a lunch meetingwith the disgraced financier on his Caribbean island in 2012. By 2015, Lutnicktried to invite Epsteinto a fundraiser for Hillary Clinton.

Lutnick in that same New York Post interview also said Epstein was blackmailing people by having them get massages and then using video of it as leverage. He even called Epstein the “greatest blackmailer ever.”

Lutnick would later testify that this amounted to just “speculating for a podcast” — not any actual knowledge of Epstein’s activities.

But it was hugely problematic for a Trump administration that had been trying to move its supporters off the Epstein conspiracy theories. Here was someone from the administration –— and Epstein’s next-door neighbor, no less — indicating one of the biggest theories was true. GOP Sen. John Kennedy even suggested that the FBI should interview Lutnick about his claims.

The White House at the time expressed confidence in Lutnick. But perhaps recognizing that his public comments often went awry, Lutnick has kept a lower public profile in 2026.

Now the magnifying glass is on him again.

Bessent said in his CNBC interview that many of the key players from the Trump administration — including the Treasury, State and Defense Departments and the US Trade Representative — wanted to designate Nvidia customer Megaspeed as a national security threat and block exports to it, over concerns that it had circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China.

Megaspeed is also the company that employed Alice Huang, with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang hadan affairand who is suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. (The US intelligence community isstill working to understandthe relationship between the Chinese businesswoman and the Chinese government.)

“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, Bessent said.

The Commerce Department announced Monday that it hadtaken a different stepto tighten export restrictions designed to prevent China from accessing the chips.

But the Commerce Department’s reluctance to take that step with Megaspeed tracks with Lutnick’s general posture favoring weaker rules for selling chips to firms that do business with China. And as theNew York Times reportedSunday, that’s a posture that also happens to help clients of the financial services firm Lutnick once led and is now led by his sons, Cantor Fitzgerald. (The Commerce Department said Lutnick has complied with all ethics agreements.)

Trump on Monday downplayed the tensions between his Cabinet secretaries, who are both traveling with him to China this week.

He said the spat between Bessent and Lutnick amounted to how “one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow up with China.”

But Bessent seemed to be gesturing at something more significant than a difference in philosophy — a Cabinet secretary allowing advanced chips to flow to a company that may be sending them to an adversary who is not supposed to have them. The Treasury secretary said that “hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage.”

And with Democrats about to have the power to subpoena people like Lutnick — and examine this or any other controversy involving his department — it’s unlikely he’ll fade into the background again.
